title: Gravitational field: force per unit mass, radial field and superposition

authority_basis.claim_scope: Gravitational field at a point is the gravitational force per unit test mass in the Newtonian model.
A point or externally equivalent spherical source produces an inward radial inverse-square field.
Newtonian gravitational-field contributions combine by vector superposition.
The near-Earth value about 9.8 N/kg is local, while gravitational field strength varies with position.

concepts.statement: The gravitational field at a point is the gravitational force per unit test mass there and, within the Newtonian test-mass model, does not depend on the chosen test mass.
concepts.why_required: Field must be separated from the force experienced by a particular object so source geometry can be studied independently of test mass.
concepts.failure_if_omitted: Learners may treat field and force as the same quantity or expect field strength to scale with the chosen test mass.

concepts.statement: For a point source or outside a spherically symmetric source, the field is radial, directed toward the source, and decreases with the inverse square of distance.
concepts.why_required: The spatial field model requires both magnitude variation and local inward direction.
concepts.failure_if_omitted: A learner may use a universal page-down direction or a constant value of g away from the near-Earth approximation.

concepts.statement: For multiple Newtonian sources, the net gravitational field at one point is the vector sum of the individual source fields evaluated at that same point.
concepts.why_required: Multi-source field problems require vector combination at one common field point rather than scalar addition of magnitudes.
concepts.failure_if_omitted: Contributions from different sources may be added without direction or evaluated at inconsistent spatial points.

model_conditions.condition: The test mass is sufficiently small that it does not materially alter the source configuration whose field is being described.
model_conditions.physical_reason: A field property should characterize the source configuration independently of the probing mass within the Newtonian test-mass model.
model_conditions.failure_consequence: The source configuration and mutual interaction must be modelled together rather than treating the field as unchanged.

model_conditions.condition: The source is a point mass or the field point lies outside a spherically symmetric source so external spherical reduction is valid.
model_conditions.physical_reason: The simple radial inverse-square field relation assumes the source mass can be represented at its centre for the field point considered.
model_conditions.failure_consequence: The field of the actual extended mass distribution must be computed using a more detailed source model.

model_conditions.condition: The Newtonian field contributions are evaluated at the same spatial point in one common coordinate frame.
model_conditions.physical_reason: Superposition combines vector field values that refer to one physical point and common basis.
model_conditions.failure_consequence: Adding vectors from different points or bases produces a quantity with no defined field meaning.

representations.semantic_geometry: Field vectors are attached to spatial sample points around a source, point inward toward the source centre, and decrease in magnitude with increasing radius.
mandatory_elements: inward-directed field vectors or field lines
must_not_imply: gravity has one absolute page-down direction
field vectors belong to the moving test object rather than spatial points
representations.verification_method: Check every vector points toward the source centre and that equal-radius points have equal magnitude under the spherical model while larger radius gives smaller magnitude.

representations.semantic_geometry: Individual source field vectors share one tail at the common field point and are combined by vector addition into one resultant field vector.
mandatory_elements: individual g_i vectors at the field point
must_not_imply: field magnitudes may be added without direction
contributions evaluated at different points can be combined directly
representations.verification_method: Resolve or geometrically add all source contributions at the same field point and check symmetry/limiting cases where one source is removed or sources are arranged symmetrically.

reasoning_sequence.expert_action: Identify the source mass model and the exact spatial field point before introducing a test mass or equation.
reasoning_sequence.failure_if_skipped: The field can be confused with a force on a particular object or evaluated at the wrong distance.

reasoning_sequence.expert_action: For each source, define radial direction and evaluate the inverse-square field contribution at the common field point.
reasoning_sequence.failure_if_skipped: Magnitude and direction can be assigned inconsistently or using an absolute down direction.

reasoning_sequence.expert_action: For multiple sources, express all field contributions in one frame at the same field point and add them vectorially.
reasoning_sequence.failure_if_skipped: Scalar magnitudes may be added despite opposing or non-collinear field directions.

reasoning_sequence.expert_action: Only after the field is known, connect it to the force on a specified mass using F_grav = m_test g and verify units, direction, symmetry and limits.
reasoning_sequence.failure_if_skipped: Field and force can remain conflated and test-mass independence can be lost.

required_transformations.description: Separate source field from force on a particular test mass by reconstructing g = F_grav / m_test and its test-mass independence.
Translate source-point geometry into an inward radial field vector with inverse-square magnitude.
Bring all source contributions to one common field point/frame and combine them by vector superposition.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Gravitational field and gravitational force are the same physical quantity and must have the same numerical value for every object.
misconceptions.why_plausible: Near Earth's surface, weight problems often use g and F together numerically without emphasizing their different units and object dependence.
trigger_contexts: different test masses at same location
misconceptions.required_counterexample: Two different test masses at the same point experience different forces but the same gravitational field in the test-mass model.
misconceptions.required_representation_repair: Show one field vector attached to the spatial point and separate force vectors on two different test masses placed there.
misconceptions.required_technical_repair: Field is force per unit mass with units N/kg or m/s^2; force on a particular mass is F_grav = m g.
misconceptions.verification: Double the test mass at fixed field point: force doubles while computed g remains unchanged.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The gravitational field strength g is universally 9.8 N/kg everywhere in space.
misconceptions.why_plausible: Introductory near-Earth problems often use a constant g approximation without foregrounding its local scope.
misconceptions.required_counterexample: Using g = GM/r^2 at two different radii gives different field magnitudes for the same source mass.
misconceptions.required_representation_repair: Plot or depict inward field vectors that visibly shorten as radius increases.
misconceptions.required_technical_repair: About 9.8 N/kg is a near-Earth-surface approximation; the external Newtonian field varies as GM/r^2.
misconceptions.verification: Check the limiting trend g -> 0 as r becomes very large.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Gravity always points toward a fixed downward direction on the page or in absolute space.
misconceptions.why_plausible: Classroom diagrams often draw local Earth gravity downward in one fixed page orientation.
misconceptions.required_counterexample: At opposite sides of a spherical planet, local gravitational-field vectors point in opposite page directions while both point toward the same centre.
misconceptions.required_representation_repair: Use radial vectors around a spherical source rather than one repeated page-down arrow.
misconceptions.required_technical_repair: For a spherical source, field direction is locally toward the source centre; page orientation is only a coordinate choice.
misconceptions.verification: Rotate the diagram or choose a different field point and confirm the field follows source-centre geometry, not page orientation.

problem_families.name: Field of a point or externally spherical source
problem_families.first_technical_move: Identify source centre and field point, define r, and set inward radial direction before calculation.
fatal_errors: measuring distance from surface instead of centre when inappropriate

problem_families.name: External gravitational field of a spherical body
problem_families.first_technical_move: Confirm the field point is outside the spherical source and use centre distance.
fatal_errors: treating near-Earth constant g as universal

problem_families.name: Multi-source gravitational-field superposition
problem_families.first_technical_move: Draw each source contribution at the same field point before adding vectors or components.

falsification_cases.authoring_defect: Remove the superposition relation while retaining the field-superposition representation.
